title: PERMA and the Science of Flourishing
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart insists that long-term flourishing, not the next high-stakes test, is the point of schooling, and he uses Martin Seligman's PERMA framework to give the idea concrete shape. He walks through positive emotion, engagement (flow), positive relationships, meaning and achievement, translating each into key questions for teachers about both their students and themselves. He argues that engagement in the flow sense is a much higher bar than the attention-getting edutainment the word usually signals. Drawing on the Harvard Grant Study, he stresses relationships as a skill to be taught through collaborative work, and he sees project-based learning as a promising route to meaning. On achievement, he resists both test obsession and knee-jerk dismissals of tests, wanting students to enjoy surmounting obstacles. He closes by cautioning against over-scientizing the framework: its value is in helping teachers think more clearly.
points: Stuart argues that long-term flourishing is the point of schooling and uses Seligman's PERMA model to make that aim concrete.
He contends that "engagement" in education usually means mere attention, whereas the flow sense of engagement is a far higher and more meaningful bar.
Each PERMA element is paired with questions for teachers about their own flourishing, such as setting work hours to protect relationships.
He resists both test obsession and knee-jerk anti-testing, wanting students to find enjoyment in surmounting obstacles and doing well.
PERMA is meant as a tool for clear thinking, not a rubric for rating students on a clipboard.
quotes: Here's why today's article matters: despite the pressure many of us feel to help our students succeed in whichever high stakes test comes next in their lives, we all got into this work because we wanted to make a long-term difference. Our Mt. Everests, when we were starting out, weren't “help my kids for the year they're with me” — they were “help my kids for the next twenty years.

It's important to me that my students experience moments of mirth when we read Romeo and Juliet (Figure 1), yet I get really excited when they've gone from loathing Shakespeare to experiencing positive emotions just by reading the play or listening to it performed by professional actors. This isn't because I'm insistent that all people love Shakespeare; it's because there's power in being able to learn to love a thing you weren't initially drawn to.

This is a high bar for a word so overused in education that it's become nearly useless. Usually, when we say “engagement” we mean that the kids are paying attention. Far too often, teachers feel like they need to entertain kids to keep them engaged. As we find ourselves slipping further into edutainment, a part of us asks, “Is this the best I can aim for? Is this what school is?
Engagement, considered this way, is much richer than something you can come to my room and observe on an evaluation day.

The cultivation of a sense of meaning, to me, is one of the most promising outcomes of project-based learning scenarios. At the end of every year in my world history courses, I love challenging my kids to formulate ways that they can make their own mark on world history — that they can see themselves as belonging to something much bigger than them.

Knee-jerk reactions to over-testing — telling or giving kids the impression that achievement on things like standardized tests just don't matter at all — trouble me. Even as I lament the insane hyper-testing happening around the country today, I still want my students to become people who can find enjoyment in surmounting obstacles and doing well at the things we put our hands to.

For what it's worth, when I come across an interesting, hard-earned idea like Seligman's and share it here on the blog, I hope you're not tempted to walk around the classroom with every kid's name on a clipboard, rating them on a scale of 1-5 for each element of PERMA. There's no need to over-science things.
